title: How To Say Hard Things In A Softer Way
summary: The creator shares a three-part framework for communicating difficult messages to senior colleagues or people with strong egos without hurting your career. The method relies on starting with positivity, adding humility, and framing your input as a question rather than a direct statement.
key_points: Do not immediately jump into what you want to say, as direct and blunt delivery can backfire and hurt your career.
Step 1: Start off with something positive, kind, or a compliment. Example: 'I know how hard you work and I know how much you do for the team.'
Step 2: Add a little bit of softness and humility. Example: 'I don't want to come across as a know-it-all.'
Step 3: Frame your point as a question rather than a statement, especially when dealing with high-ego people or those ahead of you in their career.
Example for Step 3: 'Is it okay if I suggest something that might make it easier for everyone to get their job done on time?'
The creator has successfully tested this framework across multiple industries and nationalities over nine and a half years with over 1,200 immigrants.
The lower you are on the food chain at work, the more mindful you need to be to avoid hurting your career.
You won't need this framework forever; as you build trust and familiarity over time, you can become more direct.
content: Want to say something difficult at work? Don’t say it directly. Especially if you’re talking to someone more senior than you. Use this 3-part framework instead: 1. Start positive. “Hey, I know how hard you work and how much you do for the team.” 2. Add humility. “I don’t want to come across like I know everything…” 3. Ask. Don’t tell. Instead of: “We should do this.” Say: “Would it be okay if I suggested something?” That’s it. Positive → Humility → Question. You can use this to disagree. Give feedback. Make suggestions. Or raise uncomfortable issues. I’ve trained 1,200+ immigrants over 9.5 years. And I’ve seen this work across industries and nationalities. One important thing: You won’t need this forever. The longer you work with people, the more trust you build. And the more familiar you become, the more direct you can be. But when you’re new? Or talking to someone you don’t know well? This works really well. Make a note of this post. Here’s how to say hard things in a soft, kind way, because so many times you’re going to be talking to people higher up than you, more senior than you, who have a little bit more of an ego. And if you say things in the wrong way, it can actually backfire and hurt your career. So you need to learn a simple framework that you can frame anything in a way that makes you come across as more polite and kind and friendly. And the reason I know this works is because I’ve trained over 1200 immigrants over the last nine and a half years, and this framework has worked over multiple industries, multiple nationalities. Everyone can make this work, and it's a simple three-part framework. And the first thing is, you need to start off with something positive. So what most people do is they have something that they want to say, and they immediately go into whatever they were thinking. For example, let's say you're not that high up in the food chain at work, and you want to make a suggestion to your boss. So what most people do is they go immediately into the topic, hey, this is what I think we should do. And that comes across as very blunt and direct. What you want to do instead is start off with something positive, something kind, some kind of compliment. For example, hey, I know how hard you work and I know how much you do for the team. Now, it doesn’t have to be a grand compliment, but it just needs to be subtle enough that it starts off the conversation on a good note. Then, step number two is you need to add a little bit of softness. So, for example, hey, I know how hard you work and I know how much effort you put in for the team, and I don’t want to come across as a know-it-all or an [unclear] and just by adding that one extra line of humility in the middle, you make what you say afterwards a lot more easier for them to digest. Which leads me to the last point, which is you don’t want to make statements. So what most people do is they say, hey, we should do this. And they have a lot of certainty, especially if you’re dealing with high ego people, people who are ahead of you in their career, you don’t want to make statements because you might be wrong. So the better way to do this and to also protect yourself is by framing it as a question. I know how hard you work and how much effort you put in for the team, and I don’t want to come across as an asshole. But is it okay if I suggest something that might make it easier for everyone to get their job done on time? Rather than making a statement, you say, is it okay if I share something? Because the lower you are on the food chain at work, you need to be extra mindful of not doing things that hurt your career. The higher up the food chain you get, the more direct you get to be.
